```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
library(dplyr)
covid <- read.csv("../data/covid_testing.csv") |> as_tibble()

# grading helpers
pass <- function(msg = "Nice work!") list(correct = TRUE, message = msg)
fail <- function(msg) list(correct = FALSE, message = msg)
same_df <- function(a, b) {
  is.data.frame(a) && nrow(a) == nrow(b) && ncol(a) == ncol(b) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(a), as.data.frame(b), check.attributes = FALSE))
}
not_df <- fail("Your code should return a data frame. Start with `covid |>` and don't save the result with `<-`.")
```

## The data

`covid` holds **15,524 COVID-19 tests** from the first 107 days of the pandemic at the Children's Hospital of
Philadelphia (from the `medicaldata` package). Names in the data are fake. Some of the columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `subject_id` | Person tested |
| `gender` | Gender |
| `age` | Age in years |
| `pan_day` | Day of the pandemic the test was collected (day 1 = start of data) |
| `clinic_name` | Where the sample was collected |
| `result` | `"positive"`, `"negative"`, or `"invalid"` |
| `demo_group` | `"patient"`, `"client"`, `"misc adult"`, `"other adult"`, `"unidentified"` |
| `drive_thru_ind` | 1 = collected at a drive-through site, 0 = not |
| `ct_result` | PCR cycle threshold (45 = virus not detected) |

Run this block to take a look:

```{webr}
glimpse(covid)
```

## Part 1: Is it tidy?

Remember the three rules of tidy data: each **variable** is a column, each **observation** is a row,
and each **value** is a cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Question: What is one row of `covid`? Think, then click to check.
One row is **one test**. Some people were tested more than once, so one row is *not* one person.
That matters when you count: `nrow(covid)` counts tests, not people.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Question: Imagine a table with one row per clinic and a separate column for each pandemic day's test count. Is that tidy?
No. "Day" is a variable, but in that table its values are spread across column names.
You'll learn to fix that shape with `pivot_longer()` next week.
:::

## Part 2: Working with rows

### Exercise 1: filter()

Keep only the **positive** tests.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
covid |>
  filter(result == ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex1"}
`result` is a character column, so the value goes in quotes: `"positive"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex1"}
```r
covid |>
  filter(result == "positive")
```
There are 865 positive tests.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
#| check: true
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (same_df(.result, filter(covid, result == "positive"))) {
  pass("Correct! 865 of the 15,524 tests were positive.")
} else if (nrow(.result) == 0) {
  fail("You got zero rows. Check spelling and capitalization: the value is \"positive\", all lowercase.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. You should end up with only rows where `result` is \"positive\".")
}
```

### Exercise 2: filter() with two conditions

Keep positive tests from people who are **18 or older**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
covid |>
  filter(result == "positive", ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex2"}
Separating conditions with a comma inside `filter()` means *both* must be true.
Use `>=` for "greater than or equal to."
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex2"}
```r
covid |>
  filter(result == "positive", age >= 18)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
#| check: true
target <- filter(covid, result == "positive", age >= 18)
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (same_df(.result, target)) {
  pass("Correct! 342 positive tests came from adults.")
} else if (nrow(.result) == nrow(filter(covid, result == "positive", age > 18))) {
  fail("Close. Did you use `>` instead of `>=`? 18-year-olds count.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. Keep rows that are positive AND have age of at least 18.")
}
```

### Exercise 3: arrange()

Sort the tests from **oldest to youngest** person. Look at the top of the result.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
covid |>
  select(subject_id, age, demo_group) |>
  arrange(______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex3"}
`arrange()` sorts smallest-to-largest by default. Wrap the column in `desc()` to reverse it.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex3"}
```r
covid |>
  select(subject_id, age, demo_group) |>
  arrange(desc(age))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
#| check: true
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (nrow(.result) == nrow(covid) && isTRUE(.result$age[1] == max(covid$age)) &&
           !is.unsorted(rev(.result$age))) {
  pass("Sorted! Now look at the top rows. Do those ages look believable?")
} else if (isTRUE(.result$age[1] == min(covid$age))) {
  fail("That's youngest to oldest. Use `desc(age)` to flip the order.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. Sort by `age`, largest first.")
}
```

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Think about it: what's wrong with the top rows?
The oldest "person" is 138, and several are 119. Those ages are almost certainly **data entry errors**
or placeholder values. Real data always needs a sanity check before analysis. Sorting is one of the
quickest ways to find problems.
:::

## Part 3: Working with columns

### Exercise 4: select()

Keep only the columns `subject_id`, `age`, `clinic_name`, and `result`, in that order.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
covid |>
  select(______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex4"}
List the column names inside `select()`, separated by commas. No quotes needed.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex4"}
```r
covid |>
  select(subject_id, age, clinic_name, result)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
#| check: true
want <- c("subject_id", "age", "clinic_name", "result")
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (identical(names(.result), want)) {
  pass()
} else if (setequal(names(.result), want)) {
  fail("Right columns, wrong order. List them in the order asked.")
} else {
  fail(paste0("Your columns are: ", paste(names(.result), collapse = ", "),
              ". You need: ", paste(want, collapse = ", "), "."))
}
```

### Exercise 5: mutate()

Add a new column `age_months` that is age in **months**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
covid |>
  mutate(age_months = ______) |>
  select(subject_id, age, age_months)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex5"}
There are 12 months in a year. Columns can be used in arithmetic: `age * 2`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex5"}
```r
covid |>
  mutate(age_months = age * 12) |>
  select(subject_id, age, age_months)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
#| check: true
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (!"age_months" %in% names(.result)) {
  fail("I can't find a column called `age_months`. Check the spelling on the left of `=`.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result$age_months, covid$age * 12))) {
  pass()
} else {
  fail("`age_months` has the wrong values. Multiply `age` by 12.")
}
```

## Part 4: Summarizing

### Exercise 6: count()

How many tests came from each `clinic_name`? Show the **largest first**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
covid |>
  count(clinic_name, ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex6"}
`count()` has an argument `sort`. Set it to `TRUE`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex6"}
```r
covid |>
  count(clinic_name, sort = TRUE)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
#| check: true
target <- count(covid, clinic_name, sort = TRUE)
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (same_df(.result, target)) {
  pass("Correct! The clinical lab collected the most tests (7,500).")
} else if (same_df(arrange(.result, clinic_name), arrange(target, clinic_name))) {
  fail("Right counts, but sort them so the biggest is at the top.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. Count by `clinic_name` and sort.")
}
```

### Exercise 7: group_by() + summarize()

Were drive-through tests more likely to be positive? For each value of `drive_thru_ind`, compute
the number of tests (`n`) and the percent positive (`pct_positive`).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex7
covid |>
  group_by(______) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    pct_positive = mean(result == "positive") * 100
  )
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex7"}
Group by the column that marks drive-through tests.

Why does `mean(result == "positive")` work? `result == "positive"` gives `TRUE`/`FALSE`, which R treats as 1/0.
The mean of 1s and 0s is a proportion.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex7"}
```r
covid |>
  group_by(drive_thru_ind) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    pct_positive = mean(result == "positive") * 100
  )
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex7
#| check: true
target <- covid |> group_by(drive_thru_ind) |>
  summarize(n = n(), pct_positive = mean(result == "positive") * 100)
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (same_df(.result, target)) {
  pass("Correct! About 6.0% positive at the drive-through vs. 5.1% elsewhere.")
} else if (nrow(.result) == 1) {
  fail("Only one row came back, so nothing was grouped. Fill in `group_by()`.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. Group by `drive_thru_ind`.")
}
```

### Exercise 8: your turn, from scratch

Find the **median age** for each `demo_group`. Call the summary column `median_age`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8
covid |>
  ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex8"}
Same pattern as Exercise 7: `group_by()` then `summarize()`. Use `median(age)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex8"}
```r
covid |>
  group_by(demo_group) |>
  summarize(median_age = median(age))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8
#| check: true
target <- covid |> group_by(demo_group) |> summarize(median_age = median(age))
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (same_df(.result, target)) {
  pass("Correct! Patients have a median age of 5. This is a children's hospital.")
} else if (!"median_age" %in% names(.result)) {
  fail("Name your summary column `median_age`.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. Group by `demo_group`, then summarize `median(age)`.")
}
```

## Part 5: Put it all together

### Exercise 9

Among **patients** only, and **excluding invalid** tests, what percent of tests were positive for each
gender? Round `pct_positive` to 1 decimal place.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex9
covid |>
  filter(______, ______) |>
  group_by(______) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    pct_positive = round(______, 1)
  )
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex9"}
Two conditions in `filter()`: `demo_group == "patient"` and `result != "invalid"`
(`!=` means "not equal to").
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex9"}
For the percent, reuse `mean(result == "positive") * 100` from Exercise 7.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex9"}
```r
covid |>
  filter(demo_group == "patient", result != "invalid") |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    pct_positive = round(mean(result == "positive") * 100, 1)
  )
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex9
#| check: true
target <- covid |>
  filter(demo_group == "patient", result != "invalid") |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarize(n = n(), pct_positive = round(mean(result == "positive") * 100, 1))
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  not_df
} else if (same_df(.result, target)) {
  pass("Excellent! 4.9% of tests for female patients and 4.2% for male patients were positive.")
} else if (nrow(.result) == 2 && isTRUE(sum(.result$n) != sum(target$n))) {
  fail("You have the right groups but the wrong number of tests. Check both `filter()` conditions.")
} else {
  fail("Not quite. Filter, then group by `gender`, then summarize.")
}
```

## Wrap-up

You used the five core dplyr verbs today:

| Verb | Does what to the data |
|---|---|
| `filter()` | keeps **rows** that meet a condition |
| `arrange()` | **sorts** rows |
| `select()` | keeps **columns** |
| `mutate()` | **adds** or changes columns |
| `group_by()` + `summarize()` | **collapses** each group to one row |

Next: **HW 04** practices these verbs in RStudio. The [Week 5 cheat sheet](../cheatsheets/cheatsheet-05.qmd) has all the syntax on one page.
